summary.text: The Holdridge life zones system is a global bioclimatic scheme for classifying land areas, first published by Leslie Holdridge in 1947 and updated in 1967.
It assumes that once an area's climate is known, its soil and climax vegetation can be mapped, and it starts from a measure called biotemperature.
A major use is judging how natural vegetation may shift with global warming, and fast life zone shifts bring unstable weather that poorer regions are less able to handle.

facts.label: Original focus
facts.value: Tropical and subtropical areas, now applied globally

facts.label: Biotemperature rule
facts.value: Temperatures below freezing or above 30 °C count as 0 °C

facts.label: High-emissions outlook
facts.value: 31% of crops, 34% of livestock outside safe space

facts.label: Low-emissions outlook
facts.value: 5% of crops, 8% of livestock outside safe space

items.prompt: Holdridge's biotemperature tries to capture the warmth plants can use. How does it count a stretch of days averaging 35 °C, when most plants sit dormant?
items.explain: Temperatures below freezing and above 30 °C are set to 0 °C because most plants are dormant at those temperatures.

items.prompt: A wealthy region and a region with few resources both face the same rapid shift in life zones. What does research suggest?

options.label: The wealthy region is likelier to adapt
Both regions will adapt equally well
The poorer region is likelier to adapt
Neither region's farming will be affected

items.explain: Developed regions may be able to adjust, while those with fewer resources are less likely to.

items.prompt: The coldest places on Earth are deserts. What explains this?

options.label: Winds carry all the snow out to sea
Thick ice absorbs any rain that falls
Snow is too heavy to fall from clouds there
Too little heat to evaporate much water

items.explain: With not enough heat to evaporate much water, the coldest regions get little evapotranspiration or precipitation, making polar deserts.

items.prompt: With unlimited water, a field would lose 800 mm a year to evaporation and plant transpiration. What is true of how much it actually loses?

options.label: It can top 800 mm on hot days
It can never be more than 800 mm
It equals the rainfall plus 800 mm

items.explain: The 800 mm is the potential evapotranspiration, and actual evapotranspiration can never be greater than that potential.

items.prompt: Holdridge's system leans heavily on temperature. In which kind of place would you expect it to work least well?
items.explain: The system fits tropical, Mediterranean and boreal zones but is less applicable to cold oceanic or cold arid climates where moisture dominates.

items.prompt: If greenhouse gas emissions keep rising, areas producing how much of today's crop and livestock output could see very rapid life zone shifts?
items.explain: Under the high-emissions SSP5-8.5 scenario, areas responsible for over half of current crop and livestock output would shift very rapidly.
